title: History: acute scrotal pain in a teenager

header.contentArea: Communication skills in giving and receiving information and history taking
guidelineVersions: GMC Intimate examinations and chaperones (2024; updated Dec 2024)

related.why: The examination and the painless lump

brief.scenario: Josh Radley, 14, has come in with his mother with left-sided testicular pain.
brief.task: Take a focused history from Josh and his mother. You will be stopped at 6 minutes to summarise your history, then asked about examination and immediate management.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Sudden testicular pain in a teenager is torsion until proven otherwise. The clock started when the pain did.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Talking only to the parent, or softening questions until the timing is lost.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: Speak to Josh first. "What time exactly did the pain start?"

flow: Introduce to both; speak to Josh

grid.label: Opening with a teenager and parent
grid.fail: Addresses only the mother, or uses language that embarrasses Josh.
grid.pass: Introduces to both, speaks to Josh directly, explains why he needs to ask personal questions.
grid.high: Offers Josh a chance to talk without his mother, if he'd like, and checks his mother is comfortable with that.

grid.label: Onset and timing (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Doesn't establish when the pain started.
grid.borderline: Asks "how long?" and accepts "since this morning".
grid.pass: Exact time of onset, sudden or gradual, side, severity, radiation to groin or abdomen.
grid.high: Works out the hours since onset aloud and links them to the 4–6 hour viability window.

grid.label: Associated features and differentials
grid.fail: Doesn't ask about vomiting or previous episodes.
grid.pass: Nausea and vomiting, previous similar episodes, trauma, urinary symptoms, fever, rash.
grid.high: Explains that brief self-settling episodes before suggest intermittent torsion; asks about abdominal pain as the first symptom.

grid.label: Background for theatre
grid.fail: Doesn't ask when he last ate or drank.
grid.pass: Last food and drink, medical history, medicines taken today, allergies, previous groin or scrotal surgery.
grid.high: Asks whether both testes have always been in the scrotum, and about any anaesthetic problems in the family.

grid.label: Concerns: Josh and his mother
grid.fail: Ignores Josh's embarrassment or his mother's guilt about the delay.
grid.pass: Asks both what they think is wrong and what worries them; acknowledges embarrassment.
grid.high: Takes the fertility question seriously without false promises; reassures his mother without blame.

grid.label: Summary at the signal
grid.fail: Offers epididymitis or a pulled muscle as the diagnosis.
grid.pass: Summary with time of onset; torsion until proven otherwise; differential of torsion of the appendix testis or epididymo-orchitis.
grid.high: Leads with the time since onset and says exploration is needed now.

grid.label: Examination
grid.fail: Examines without a chaperone, or relies on a sign to rule out torsion.
grid.pass: Offers a trained chaperone; normal side first; lie, height, tenderness, cremasteric reflex; abdomen and hernial orifices.
grid.high: States that his mother is a support, not a chaperone, and that no single sign excludes torsion.

grid.label: Immediate management (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Arranges an ultrasound first, or sends him home with antibiotics.
grid.borderline: Calls urology but asks for an ultrasound first "to confirm".
grid.pass: Immediate referral for scrotal exploration; nil by mouth; analgesia; no delay for imaging.
grid.high: Explains consent: possible orchidectomy and fixation of the other testis; Doppler flow doesn't exclude torsion.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Hi Mum, what's the problem with him?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: So he's had pain down there since this morning. Any burning when he wees?

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Please stop there and summarise your history.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Josh is 14 with left testicular pain since this morning. Probably epididymitis.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: How would you examine him, and what next?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd have a quick feel while his mum's there, and if the cremasteric reflex is present it isn't torsion. I'd get an ultrasound and start antibiotics.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Hello, I'm Dr Lin, one of the surgical doctors. Are you Josh? And you're his mum? Josh, I need to ask some personal questions so we can work out what's wrong. Is that OK?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: What time did the pain start? Did it come on suddenly? Which side? How bad, out of ten? Does it spread anywhere?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Have you felt sick or been sick? Ever had pain like this before? Any knock or injury? Any burning when you pass urine, a temperature or a rash?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: When did you last eat or drink? Any illnesses or operations? Any medicines today? Any allergies?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: What do you both think is going on? What's worrying you most? It's completely normal to feel embarrassed.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Please stop there and summarise your history.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Josh is 14. Sudden severe left testicular pain woke him at 4 am, with vomiting. He had a short similar episode two months ago. This is testicular torsion until proven otherwise; the differential is torsion of the appendix testis or epididymo-orchitis.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd offer a chaperone. I'd examine the right side first, then the left: lie, height, tenderness and the cremasteric reflex. Then the abdomen and hernial orifices.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: The left testis is high, horizontal and very tender. What next?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd call the urology registrar now for scrotal exploration, without waiting for a scan. He stays nil by mouth, and I'd give him pain relief.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Hello, I'm Dr Lin, one of the surgical doctors. Are you Josh? And you're his mum? Josh, if you'd like to talk to me on your own for any of this, that's fine; is that OK with you, Mrs Radley?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: So it woke you at 4, and it's half seven now: three and a half hours. That matters, because the sooner it's sorted, the better the chance of saving the testicle.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Did it start in your tummy? You said it happened before and went away on its own: that can mean the testicle twisted and untwisted.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Have both testicles always been down in the scrotum? Anyone in the family had problems with an anaesthetic?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: You asked about having children one day. That's a really sensible question, and the best thing for it is getting you sorted quickly; the surgeon will talk it through with you. Mrs Radley, you did the right thing bringing him in.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Please stop there and summarise your history.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Josh is 14 with sudden left testicular pain, three and a half hours old, with vomiting and a previous self-settling episode. This is torsion until proven otherwise, and he needs exploration now.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd offer a trained chaperone; Mum can stay as support, but she isn't a chaperone. Normal side first, then the left. I'd note the lie and the cremasteric reflex, but no single sign rules torsion out.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The left testis is high, horizontal and very tender. What next?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Urology now for exploration: the testis is most likely to survive if it's untwisted within 4 to 6 hours of onset. Nil by mouth and IV analgesia. The surgeon will consent Josh and his mum for untwisting, possible removal, and fixing the other side. A Doppler with flow wouldn't exclude torsion, so I wouldn't wait for one.

failures.move: Not pinning down the time of onset.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: the time since onset drives the urgency, and delay costs the testis.

failures.move: Waiting for an ultrasound before calling urology.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: exploration takes precedence over imaging when torsion is suspected.

failures.move: Using his mother as the chaperone, or a present cremasteric reflex to exclude torsion.
failures.consequence: A relative is not an impartial chaperone, and no single sign rules out torsion.

failures.move: Talking over Josh to his mother.
failures.consequence: A teenager who is embarrassed and ignored holds back symptoms, including earlier episodes.

recovery.when: You didn't get an exact time
recovery.line: Can we be really precise: what time did the pain wake you?
Doctors ask these questions every day. Would it be easier to talk without your mum for a moment?

knowledge.fact: Testis most likely viable if treated within 4–6 hours of pain onset; beyond 10–12 hours irreversible damage is likely (1.1.4).

Suspected torsion: immediate surgical consultation and exploration take precedence over tests (1.3.2); sudden one-sided testicular pain is the key feature, even when abdominal pain or vomiting dominate (5.3.4).
Persistent arterial flow on Doppler does not exclude torsion; contralateral fixation is commonly done at the same operation.
A relative is not usually a suitable chaperone (para 20).
A young person's capacity to consent depends on understanding, not age; encourage parental involvement (paras 24–25, 29).

recall.think: Torsion: a testis lost to delay.
recall.say: "Torsion until proven otherwise; he needs exploration now."

numbers.meaning: from onset: testis most likely viable

recall.trap: A present cremasteric reflex or Doppler flow reassures.
recall.finish: Scrotal exploration; untwist or remove; fix both sides.

sources.name: ICBSE Guide to the intercollegiate MRCS examination
sources.supports: Station format: 9-minute stations with 1 minute's reading; introduce yourself and confirm identity at every station

sources.name: HSIB (now HSSIB) national investigation: Management of acute onset testicular pain
sources.supports: If treatment starts within four to six hours of pain onset the testicle will most likely remain viable; if twisting lasts more than 10 to 12 hours, irreversible damage is likely (1.1.4, 1.4.1); history of intermittent pain may indicate torsion and spontaneous untwisting; often no relief on elevating the scrotum (1.3.1); when history and examination suggest torsion, immediate surgical consultation and exploration take precedence over diagnostic tests (1.3.2); after untwisting or removal, the other testicle is usually fixed (1.4.1); ages 12 to 18 at greater risk (1.5.1); sudden-onset unilateral testicular pain is the most obvious indicator, whether or not abdominal pain or nausea and vomiting dominate; the most effective diagnostic procedure is emergency scrotal exploration, not a scan or the cremasteric reflex (5.3.4)

sources.name: European Association of Urology / ESPU Guidelines on Paediatric Urology, chapter: Acute scrotum
sources.supports: Critical window of approximately four to six hours; base the diagnosis on physical examination; Doppler ultrasound is useful but must not delay intervention; persistent arterial flow does not exclude torsion; residual torsion found at exploration in patients who reported pain relief after manual detorsion; contralateral orchidopexy commonly performed immediately after detorsion; perform urgent surgical exploration as soon as possible

sources.name: GMC: Intimate examinations and chaperones
sources.version: In effect from 30 January 2024; updated 13 December 2024
sources.supports: Explain the examination and that the patient can stop it (para 8); consent or other valid authority, recorded (para 9); children and young people: assess capacity, otherwise parental consent (para 11); offer an impartial chaperone (para 16); a relative or friend is not usually a suitable chaperone (para 20); record the chaperone discussion and identity (para 23)

sources.name: GMC: 0–18 years: guidance for all doctors
sources.version: In effect 15 October 2007; updated 25 May 2018 and 13 December 2024
sources.supports: Emergency treatment without consent to save life or prevent serious deterioration (para 22); involve children and young people as much as possible (para 23); capacity depends on the ability to understand and weigh up options more than on age (paras 24–25); if a child lacks capacity, ask a parent; one parent is usually enough (para 27); encourage young people to involve their parents in important decisions (para 29)

partner.opening: Please take a focused history from Josh and his mother. I'll stop you at 6 minutes to summarise.
partner.actorBrief: Two actors. Josh Radley, 14, in Year 9, plays football. Opening line (to the floor): "It's my… down there. It really hurts." Emotional state: in pain, embarrassed, gives short answers unless the candidate talks to him directly and kindly. Mrs Claire Radley, his mother: worried, guilty that she gave him ibuprofen and waited. Release facts only when asked (see reveals). Josh's hidden worry, said only if asked what worries him: "Will I still be able to have kids?" If offered time alone, Josh says there's nothing else, but thanks the candidate. Mrs Radley's cue: "I should have brought him in sooner."

reveals.trigger: Asks what time it started and how
reveals.finding: Josh: "It woke me up at 4. Really suddenly." He told his mum at 6.30. Left side, 9 out of 10.

reveals.trigger: Asks about spread or abdominal pain
reveals.finding: "At first I thought it was my stomach, low down on the left."
Two months ago, similar pain for about half an hour after football; it went away, and he told no one.

reveals.trigger: Asks about injury, urine, fever, rash
reveals.finding: No injury, no urinary symptoms, no fever, no rash.

reveals.trigger: Asks about last food or drink, history, medicines, allergies
reveals.finding: A slice of toast and squash at 6.30 am. Well; no operations; ibuprofen 400 mg at 6.30 am; no allergies. Both testes "always been there".

reveals.trigger: Asks Mrs Radley what worries her
reveals.finding: "I gave him ibuprofen and told him to see how it went. I should have brought him in sooner."
Say: "Please stop there and summarise your history."

push.question: How would you examine him? (Once answered, give the findings: left testis high-riding with a horizontal lie, swollen and exquisitely tender; left cremasteric reflex absent; right testis normal; abdomen soft; hernial orifices normal.)
push.expect: Trained chaperone offered; normal side first; lie, height, tenderness, cremasteric reflex; abdomen and hernial orifices.

push.question: What is your immediate management?
push.expect: Immediate urology referral for scrotal exploration; nil by mouth; analgesia; no delay for imaging.

push.question: What will the surgeon consent him for?
push.expect: Exploration, untwisting and fixation; possible orchidectomy; fixation of the other side.

curveballs.prompt: The ED registrar asks you to get an ultrasound first.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Explain that exploration takes precedence over imaging in suspected torsion, and escalate to the urology registrar now.

curveballs.prompt: The pain suddenly eases while you wait.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Still explore: it may have untwisted and can twist again, and pain relief doesn't exclude residual torsion, which has been found even after successful manual detorsion.

curveballs.prompt: Josh asks you not to tell his mum about the previous episode.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Respect his wish where possible; explain it matters to the surgeon, and encourage him to let you share it.
